title: Dangerous ozone threatened half of world’s population this year
summary:
This exposure reflects an intersection of climate change, air pollution and public health, says new analysisAround half of the global population has been exposed to dangerous levels of ground-level ozone this year, a new report finds.
Though ozone high up in Earth’s stratosphere provides protection from ultraviolet radiation to people and other life on the planet, ground-level ozone is a toxic pollutant.
It’s the main ingredient in smog and can cause lung damage and harm vegetation such as crops.
Both categories exceed the World Health Organization’s guidelines for exposure to the pollutant.
The CAMS report noted that both the ozone and the pollutants that lead to it can move across international borders, which makes reining it in a more difficult task.

title: Young minds in Ipswich develop ideas to tackle climate change
summary:
A group of young people have developed ideas to tackle the effects of climate change as part of a free touring exhibition.
On Tuesday 16 young people took part in a hackathon - a timed event where people work together to build creative solutions to problems - where they devised posters with ways to combat light pollution, wild fires, damage to oceans and poor water quality.
The event was hosted by Seeds of Hope and Change, an organisation run by the Soka Gakkai International and the UN Earth Charter, at the Jerwood Dancehouse in Ipswich.
Maryanne, 16, took part in the project and said: "We just want people to be aware of what's going on, especially with major issues such as ocean pollution."

title: How climate change is altering petrichor, the glorious smell after it rains
summary:
The distinct, earthy smell that fills the air after rain following a long dry spell can trigger some serious nostalgia.
But as climate change alters Earth’s weather and environment, petrichor is going to transform, too.
During dry periods, soil-dwelling bacteria produce a compound called geosmin that deters insects such as fruit flies.
Droughts cause geosmin to build up, and when they occur with hotter temperatures, bacteria produce even more geosmin as heat speeds up chemical reactions inside the microbes.
But if soils get too dry, “the geosmin will dry up and not be released,” Lundström says.

title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss
summary:
Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.

title: Swiss glaciers suffer another year of record ice loss

For years, his research has documented rapid ice loss, with the decline peaking in 2022, when Switzerland recorded a record 6% loss in a single year.

Ominously, though, Huss' research shows that individual glaciers, among them Switzerland's biggest, like the mighty Rhône and Aletsch, have suffered record ice loss this year.
